Beware the copier

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Have you copied any sensitive documents lately? There's every possibility that those documents still exist on the hard drive inside the copier you used.

Summary:
Have you copied any sensitive documents lately? There's every possibility that those documents still exist on the hard drive inside the copier you used.

Remember when copiers were simple—just paper in, copies out? Once they began scanning and faxing, copiers evolved not just in capability, but as a serious security risk.
Buried in your copier is a hard drive used to create an image of the original page that is then sent to a folder, attached to an e-mail, or sent by fax. Over 20,000 images can stay on the drive long after you have walked away.

If the drive is not removed from the copier when your lease is up or if you replace it, or if a repair includes the replacement of the drive, your old drive can become an expensive data breach.

It is relatively simple to retrieve the information stored on hard drives in copiers – and sensitive information about companies, individuals and government departments is there for the taking.


Further information:
Have you copied any sensitive documents lately? There's every possibility that those documents still exist on the hard drive inside the copier you used.

Remember when copiers were simple—just paper in, copies out? Once they began scanning and faxing, copiers evolved not just in capability, but as a serious security risk.
Buried in your copier is a hard drive used to create an image of the original page that is then sent to a folder, attached to an e-mail, or sent by fax. Over 20,000 images can stay on the drive long after you have walked away.

If the drive is not removed from the copier when your lease is up or if you replace it, or if a repair includes the replacement of the drive, your old drive can become an expensive data breach.

It is relatively simple to retrieve the information stored on hard drives in copiers – and sensitive information about companies, individuals and government departments is there for the taking.

Many enterprise-level network printers use internal hard drives to store and prioritize print jobs. Some offer PIN printing--a security feature that lets users send a print job to the printer but postpone the actual printing until they physically enter a PIN code at the printer. This feature is intended to prevent casual viewing of printed documents. Ironically it can also mean that a copy of that same sensitive document remains exposed on the printer's hard drive.


What about home copiers and all-in-one printers? They are also vulnerable to this kind of security breach. If you sell or give away an old printer, are you giving away the tax returns and personal letters you printed?

We have obtained a few hard drive from trashed office printers and have indeed found sensitive documents by the thousands on the hard drives.

Very few people know that the office copiers retains information and can pose a serious security breach -- on company level and personal level. This does not only apply to copiers used in offices but if you copy sensitive documents at Postnet or a library or internet cafe, those copiers have the data on their hard drives. It is relatively simple for a competitor or even an identity thief to retrieve the info.

The same goes for used Smart Phones, routers, GPS's -- you give and awful lot of info away when you sell or discard these devices. Even if a factory reset has been done, it is possible to retrieve an amazing amount of personal and business data.

Press Release:


Beware the Copier
One of the most serious cyber security threats an organisation faces could come from an unlikely source: the innocuous photocopier in the hallway. It’s the last device most organisations guard against security breaches or think to secure. And, as Carte Blanche reveals, the secrets it holds make it a perfect cyber crime target.


Script:


V/O:
An intruder is caught on CCTV footage, breaking into a company’s head office. But he is not after the antique bicycle in the foyer….or the flat screen TV or …….theKruger Rands in the safe. He is after another kind of gold. The gold of the information age – data.

And this gold is not found locked away, but left out in the open in the office, in this machine – the trusted office photocopier. It only takes a few minutes and a simple screwdriver to get at the coveted prize……the hard drive within.
Basie:
Every modern photocopier or multifunction device has got a hard disk in there. Every copy you make, every fax you send or receive, every confidential document you scan and send to somebody else, a copy is actually stored on the hard disk of that copy machine.
V/O:
And this makes the office copier a potential security risk, says Prof Basie von Solms - Director of the Centre for Cyber Security at the University of Johannesburg.

When copiers first arrived on the scene and revolutionized office workflows they were simple duplicating machines. It was just a matter of paper in, paper out.

But since those early days, photocopiers have evolved into sophisticated devices with data-storage capabilities. And the fact that they store all this information makes them a very real cyber security threat.
LINK
And this is the culprit – a simple hard drive, similar to what is found in laptops. They range from 40 Gig to more than 300 Gig.
V/O:
Peter Fryer is a forensics expert who specializes in the recovery of data from digital storage devices. He says it is quite easy to access a the hard drive or a modern office photocopier.
Peter
This is the multifunction that we referred to and in the back… if I open this panel…. so you can see here’s a hard drive in back and this particular drive has a capacity of 80 Gigs which will be able to store quite a couple of thousands of documents and images off of this machine.
V/O:
When copiers are traded-in or sold, the hard drives, along with thousands of stored images and files, are also passed on to a new owner. These drives could contain secret or highly sensitive information about a company or individuals.

To prove the ease with which sensitive information can be accessed we obtained a few used copier hard drives from an e-waste facility in Johannesburg and gave them to Peter to analyse.
V/O:
The intricate analysis began in his forensic laboratory.

UPSOUND DEREK
And this is it. This is the lab.

Peter showed us some of the hardware used to extract information from drives. This included an array of connectors, some sophisticated electronic devices and forensic software.
Peter:
In your hand, that hard drive is 320 Gig which in today’s terms is not a lot of data but it could still be tens of thousands of photos, documents, e-mails, and somebody just has to process that data.
Derek:
Now we get to the crucial part and actually you showing us what you found from the devices we gave you.
Peter:
Yes, most definitely and the hard drive that you are holding there, holds some nice data.
Derek:
Ok, let’s go through.
V/O
We watched in amazement as Peter revealed the extent of the data he was able to recover from the drives we had given him.
Peter
This is it. All images you can see, schedules associated with what appears to be a tender. In this instance it looks on face value to be a response to a bid by Escom. So you can see the Escom details there. ….…………….data breach or data leak.
Derek
It looks like a mining application?
Peter:
It could be a mining application. It is certainly a response to a request for a tender.
Derek:
It is incredible. It is everything that was out there.
Peter:
And the fact that I have it in this format means that I can reproduce it and print it, again. And in all likelihood this particular machine would have been standing in an open area. I doubt that the printer would have been part of the security planning around data breach or data leak.
V/O:
Peter came to this conclusion because it was clear from the images we found that the machine had also been used by employees for personal reasons. These are documents copied or scanned by somebody applying for a loan from a bank.
Peter:
You can see that it does contain some user identifiable information: signatures, account numbers, ID numbers, amounts.
V/O:
But we don’t only use copiers at work or at home. The ease of copying personal or sensitive documents at public facilities is certainly convenient - but at what security risk? When we walk away, our personal information remains on the hard drives of these communal machines. Anyone accessing their hard drives would have instant access to an individual’s bank statements, proof of residence, identity documents and other personal information. It’s an identity thief’s dream.

And there are other instances where copiers are prime targets for cyber criminals.
Basie:
The place where cyber criminals now get a lot of information is at the business centres of big conferences where a lot of important people go to the conference then they want to make a copy or scan a document or whatever so they go to the business centre. So the bad guys try and infect the computers and scanners and copiers at the business centre before the time and then they just make copies of those documents.
Derek
This is a huge wake. This is a huge security risk.
Peter
Well, for Bob Smith whose finance application we found I am sure it is.
V/O:
The industry is aware of the vulnerabilities of multifunction devices, and suppliers provide information on how to safeguard the hard drives.
Peter:
Most manufacturers do provide you with a security kit of sorts. It is a user activated function which would allow for the hard drive to be wiped ate the machine is switched off every time.
Basie:
If you set up it up from day one when you install the machine and you have security in mind and you select settings like encrypt every document before you store it on the disk, and you give pass words and you change the passwords regularly, then it is not as easy as it sounds, but most people don’t do that.
V/O
So without these measures in place, the copy machine in the hallway can be a gold mine of sensitive information.

Documents are stored in different file formats on copier drives and some of these formats even make forgery a piece of cake.
Peter:
The research I undertook on this level is that if that file type is present, it means I can reproduce original documents, or if I am up to no good I might be wanting to print a letterhead of the company and in all likelihood I might have a scanned copy of the CEO’s signature so I could give myself a raise or promotion.
V/O:
What is stored on a drive also provides some insight into the private lives of employees. One of the drives we had analysed contained copied instructions detailing the steps needed to build a model airplane. And, that was not all.
Peter:
One of the other drives we got access to we determined belonged to a church and on this drive we found a funeral notice that has been printed, but ion the same drive there was aslo financial information that was available in the form of bank statements and some invoices.
Derek:
Relating to the church?
Peter:
Relating to the church.
V/O:
Peter had used specialized forensic software to analyse drives, but it is also quite simple for criminals to get hold of software that can unlock a hard drive.
Basie:
You can find lots of programmes on the internet that can read disks, you can download software that can do that, you can even download software that can help you break the encryption key of the disk if it is encrypted. It is not rocket science anymore.
V/O:
This means that the security measures accompanying photocopy machines may fall short, should their hard drives fall into the wrong hands. So what is the solution?
Basie:
If you sell your photocopy machine make sure that the disk is wiped in a forensic proper way. And not even that. Make sure that yout It department, or a regular basis, once a week, come and visit your photocopy machine and wipe the information.
V/O:
There are also more extreme solutions.
Peter:
There is a whole subset of security tools that have emerged around cleaning and destroying hard drives. One of the mechanisms would be degauzing a hard drive where unltr high magnetism is applied to the drive which in essence would destroy the data on the drive. And in fact there are industrial shredders where you throw the drive into and small little metal pellets would come out the other end and that would certainly take care of any data stored on the device.

metadata.Further information: Have you copied any sensitive documents lately? There's every possibility that those documents still exist on the hard drive inside the copier you used. Remember when copiers were simple—just paper in, copies out? Once they began scanning and faxing, copiers evolved not just in capability, but as a serious security risk. Buried in your copier is a hard drive used to create an image of the original page that is then sent to a folder, attached to an e-mail, or sent by fax. Over 20,000 images can stay on the drive long after you have walked away. If the drive is not removed from the copier when your lease is up or if you replace it, or if a repair includes the replacement of the drive, your old drive can become an expensive data breach. It is relatively simple to retrieve the information stored on hard drives in copiers – and sensitive information about companies, individuals and government departments is there for the taking. Many enterprise-level network printers use internal hard drives to store and prioritize print jobs. Some offer PIN printing--a security feature that lets users send a print job to the printer but postpone the actual printing until they physically enter a PIN code at the printer. This feature is intended to prevent casual viewing of printed documents. Ironically it can also mean that a copy of that same sensitive document remains exposed on the printer's hard drive. What about home copiers and all-in-one printers? They are also vulnerable to this kind of security breach. If you sell or give away an old printer, are you giving away the tax returns and personal letters you printed? We have obtained a few hard drive from trashed office printers and have indeed found sensitive documents by the thousands on the hard drives. Very few people know that the office copiers retains information and can pose a serious security breach -- on company level and personal level. This does not only apply to copiers used in offices but if you copy sensitive documents at Postnet or a library or internet cafe, those copiers have the data on their hard drives. It is relatively simple for a competitor or even an identity thief to retrieve the info. The same goes for used Smart Phones, routers, GPS's -- you give and awful lot of info away when you sell or discard these devices. Even if a factory reset has been done, it is possible to retrieve an amazing amount of personal and business data.
